## P18-22 - Urban Reign group special attacks (researched 2026-11-07)

See also the Urban Reign notes of P1-01 above.

Task: how two fighters attack one target together (one holding, the other hitting), how it starts, its cost, its timing, how the target gets out, how the AI partner joins, how it looks on screen; plus 2 to 3 contrasting brawler mechanics. Facts are in our own words. No English-language source found prints a full move list or frame data, so the exact inputs, timings and the partner AI rules are "unknown" below and are not guessed. Nothing here changes the game code. Standard web search plus page fetches; several pages (GameSpot, IGN, GameFAQs guides, Sega Retro, Hardcore Gaming 101) were blocked, empty or moved, so those were not read.

#### Urban Reign (Namco, PS2, 2005): what the sources say
- Genre and setup: a 3D street brawler with Tekken-like strikes and wrestling-style grapples; story missions are fights against groups of thugs (up to five fighters on screen) or one-on-one boss fights, and many missions let the player bring a partner who must first be unlocked through the story. Source: https://www.videogamer.com/reviews/urban-reign-review , https://www.gamecheatsfinder.com/2022/02/24/urban-reign-retro-review-frustratingly-fun/60/ . Verified: yes (two reviews agree).
- Two kinds of partner moves exist and must not be mixed up: (a) "double-team" moves that need both fighters, and (b) each character's own "multi-enemy special" that hits several enemies at once. Sources: https://gamezone.com/reviews/urban_reign_ps2_review (search summary of the page; the page itself returned 404 on a later fetch), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Reign (group attacks that hit several opponents at once). Verified: partly.
- What a double-team looks like: described as tag-team wrestling pairs, for example a two-man suplex, a "you hold him and I break his ribs" strike while the partner holds the target, and a launch where one fighter tosses the enemy up and the partner catches and slams him on the pavement. Later lists name double finishers (double cutter, double super kick, a combined chair-drop and backbreaker). Sources: https://www.gamesradar.com/urban-reign/ (quote found only in the search summary, the review text itself was cut off when fetched), https://www.gamepressure.com/games/urban-reign/z71acb (toss-and-catch, fetched), https://www.gamecheatsfinder.com/2022/02/24/urban-reign-retro-review-frustratingly-fun/60/ . Verified: partly (the examples come from reviews, not a move list; the named finishers are from one search summary and are unconfirmed).
- Trigger: the reviewer of GameZone says you stand next to an enemy while the partner is near, then press Triangle. Another control listing (search snippet only, not fetched) gives Circle as strike, Triangle as grapple, Square as dodge, X as run, R1 as lock-on and R2 as the partner command, and a retro review says R2 gives teammate commands. Kikizo says you can interrupt your own attack to call the partner over to help. So the trigger is a proximity plus a command, not a long input. Sources: https://gamezone.com/reviews/urban_reign_ps2_review , https://www.gamecheatsfinder.com/2022/02/24/urban-reign-retro-review-frustratingly-fun/60/ , https://games.kikizo.com/reviews/ps2/urban_reign.asp . Verified: partly (button names disagree between sources; treat all as unknown).
- Availability: double-team moves are unlocked as the story goes on (with air grapples, wall-hop attacks and more specials). A reviewer says the team attack can be used only now and then and is "never really necessary". Sources: https://www.gamecheatsfinder.com/2022/02/24/urban-reign-retro-review-frustratingly-fun/60/ , https://www.videogamer.com/reviews/urban-reign-review . Verified: yes (two reviews).
- Cost and meter: no source says a double-team costs meter. The separate "Special Arts" move needs a meter that fills when you hit, dodge or take damage, drains on use, and can only be stopped by another special. A specials-only meter, not a team meter. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Reign , https://sites.google.com/view/methodtomadness/main/stuff-i-like/30-things-i-like-12-urban-reign , https://www.gamecheatsfinder.com/2022/02/24/urban-reign-retro-review-frustratingly-fun/60/ . Verified: yes for the specials meter, unknown for any team cost.
- Timing: no source gives startup, hold length or damage numbers. Unknown.
- How a target gets out: the target is a thug who can be countered or dodged with the one dodge/counter button. A review says if you are on the receiving end of a double team you can answer with a "counter double-team grapple"; another says a lone fighter can turn the tables with an attack that hits both attackers, if the timing is right. Reviewers also complain that when you are double-teamed or juggled the escape is mostly a timing guess and you often just take the damage and can lose the mission. Escaping grabs needs a precise reversal timing like a wrestling game (no instant tech button as in Tekken). Sources: https://www.gamecheatsfinder.com/2022/02/24/urban-reign-retro-review-frustratingly-fun/60/ , https://sites.google.com/view/methodtomadness/main/stuff-i-like/30-things-i-like-12-urban-reign (double-team counters exist), GameZone summary above (the two-attackers counter). Verified: partly (the counter for two attackers is described, not measured).
- What the AI partner does: partners are computer-controlled and mostly fight their own mini battle in the area rather than working closely with you; the player can call them over, give orders, and can switch roles and take control of the partner mid-fight. The partner running out of health does not end the mission, so it is an assist and not a thing to protect. Sources: https://www.videogamer.com/reviews/urban-reign-review , https://games.kikizo.com/reviews/ps2/urban_reign.asp , https://civilwarfare101.blogspot.com/2024/06/urban-reign-review.html . Verified: partly (no source describes the partner's decision rules).
- On screen: attacks are staged as paired wrestling animations; an early preview calls them "devastatingly impactful". No source describes a prompt, camera cut or HUD marker. Source: https://games.kikizo.com/news/200506/065.asp . Verified: partly.
- Reception: the team attack was seen as a nice extra but not needed, and the game's weakness was imprecise counters, so the lesson for us is that the move must be readable and have a clear way out. Sources: videogamer and gamecheatsfinder pages above. Verified: yes (opinion).

#### Contrast mechanics in other brawlers
- Streets of Rage 4 (Dotemu, 2020): co-op moves between two players. A free update added a move where one player grabs the partner and throws them; the thrown partner can press a button in the air for a special hit. Later patches changed it so the partner goes airborne straight away. Reviewers found the ground version fun but hard to land and had trouble with the air one; friendly fire is on by default. Lesson: a two-person move that needs both people to press at the right time is fiddly. Source: https://co-optimus.com/article/17229/free-streets-of-rage-4-update-adds-co-op-moves-custom-survival-mode-and-more.html and a search summary of https://segaretro.org/Streets_of_Rage_4 (the page itself was blocked). Verified: partly (details from search summaries, not read in full).
- Def Jam: Fight for NY (EA, 2004): the crowd does the helping. A grapple next to a spectator can start a tag-team throw with that person, and some spectators hold a fighter in place so the other fighter can hit freely. A double team with a spectator is also one of the ways to finish a low-health opponent. A Momentum meter filled by good play and counters powers a character-specific "Blazin" finisher. Lesson: the second attacker can be a neutral actor that exists by place, not by a team roster. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam:_Fight_for_NY . Verified: yes (fetched).
- Dead or Alive tag modes: an existing entry (Appendix B, P1-01) already records tag throws for pairs and a partner striking on entry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_or_Alive_(franchise) . Verified: partly (see P1-01).

#### Inputs for P18-23
Findings that shape our own design (our design must be our own: do not copy Urban Reign's move names, input names, art or text).
1. One simple rule fits the sources: the group attack is an extra option on a hold the game already has, started by the same Grapple button, not a separate system. Urban Reign needs only a nearby partner and one button; reviewers still found escapes unclear, so ours must have a fixed, visible way out.
2. Our engine already has the holding half. `Combat.startClinch` (`breakpoint.html:7241`) puts the attacker in `S.GRAPPLE` and the victim in `S.CLINCH` with `partner` links; the holder may strike twice (`CLINCH_STRIKE_MAX`, `CLINCH_MOVES` knee and elbow) or throw; the victim escapes after `CLINCH_ESCAPE_FROM` ticks if it has `ESCAPE_STAMINA` (`tryEscape`, `:6257`); a hold times out at `CLINCH_MAX` (110 ticks). The missing half is the second fighter hitting the held one: `Combat.strikable` (`:6934`) refuses any attack on a fighter in `S.CLINCH` or `S.GRAPPLE`, and `evaluate` refuses a third fighter on a submission victim (`pinnedBy`). `strikable` also gates thrown items (`:10335`, `:10346`) and thrown bodies (`:10405`), so the exception belongs in `evaluate`, for strikes by the holder's teammate, not in `strikable`; P18-23 decides whether items and thrown bodies may hit a held fighter (suggested: no). A group attack is therefore a deliberate, narrow exception: a teammate of the holder may hit the held fighter, nobody else may. P18-23 must decide the exact scope (only the holder's teammates, only one extra hit at a time, which fighters may join).
3. Determinism: all of it can sit inside the fixed 60 Hz tick with `simRng` and ticks, using the existing `partner` links, hit lists and `Events`. The extra hit needs no new randomness. The second fighter must be chosen deterministically (nearest teammate by the fighter order, ties by index) so replays and online agree. The held fighter stays in `S.CLINCH`, so the existing escape window stays the way out; P18-23 should decide whether a group hit lengthens the hold (suggest: it does not extend `CLINCH_MAX`, it spends the hold's strike count or has its own count) and whether the escape cost or window changes while a teammate is hitting (Urban Reign's complaint says: keep the window, make it clear).
4. Allies and AI (P18-21): rules decided for allies are CPU fighters on `TEAM_PLAYERS` that take no orders and cannot be swapped into, steered by `AIController` (`:8482`) at the run's CPU level (Appendix C, P18-20 + P18-37). So "one holds while the other hits" must work without commands: the AI ally sees a teammate holding (`f.state === S.GRAPPLE` with `partner` set) and joins on its own with a short delay and a cooldown, and the AI holder can wait for a nearby teammate with a limited look-ahead; humans trigger it only by what they already do (grab). Keep `canHurt` (`:9945`): teammates do not hurt each other unless Free Fight friendly fire is on (`match.friendlyFire`, `:9767`); P18-23 decides whether the helper's hit can touch the holder then (suggested: the group hit lands only on the held fighter, and only if the helper may hurt it). Enemy goons in a group (P18-21) can do the same to a player, which must be balanced like the other group rules (goon health and damage factors) and capped (one group hold at a time; a player should never be held and hit with no way out).
5. Controls, mobile first: no new on-screen button. The trigger is the existing Grapple input, pressed by the holder as today; the helper joins automatically if a teammate is within a fixed range and in a legal state, or presses Grapple again within a short window after the hold starts (keyboard, gamepad and touch need no change). A cooldown per fighter stops chaining. The tutorial/tip shows once and is saved in Progress (existing `seenClinch` style flag). Whether a human second player can join manually (co-op, up to 4 seats) is a P18-23 decision; Urban Reign's R2-style partner command is not needed since P1-03 rejected orders.
6. Modern Urban theme: a plain street double-team (one pins or locks the target, the other kicks, knees or drives them into a wall or prop) fits; stage-hazard finishes can reuse the existing ring-out and hazard code. No wrestling-ring gimmicks, no supernatural moves.
7. Cost and balance: Urban Reign has no team cost, only a specials meter. Options for P18-23: free but gated by the hold (it only exists while holding), a per-fighter cooldown, or a share of the existing momentum meter (`gainMomentum`, `MOMENTUM_PER_DAMAGE`; the ultimate in P18-08 is a separate decision). Suggest the cooldown form first because it needs no new UI. Measure with `BREAKPOINT.simulate` against the P14-01 group ladder after the P18-21 balance work so goons do not get a free kill.
8. Presentation: the paired animation need only reuse the clinch poses (`CLINCH_STRIKE_POSES`, `clinchStrikePose`) plus one extra pose for the helper; a short hit-stop (`match.hitStop`, already 4 on a clinch) and the existing event/sound hooks give the "impact" the reviews praise. The held fighter's escape prompt must stay visible so the player can read the way out.
9. Size: the budget is now 4,000,000 LF bytes (owner, 2026-11-07; the file is about 1,178,607), so size is a minor note and not a limit. A first estimate for the feature is a few KB (helper state, range test, strike rule exception, AI hook, one pose, tests). It still should reuse the clinch code instead of copying it (DRY).
10. Open questions for P18-23: (a) may two enemies group-attack one player; (b) must the holder be a human or an ally, or any fighter; (c) one extra hit or a short chain; (d) is the escape harder (more stamina) while two attackers are on you, or the same; (e) is there a counter that hits both attackers, as one review mentions; (f) cooldown length; (g) does it count in `Progress` stats and grades; (h) tests: `breakpoint-tests.js` needs the eligibility, the deterministic helper choice, the damage rule, the escape window and the no-friendly-fire cases, each as its own self-test.

## P18-26 - Mobile release and free-to-play (researched 2026-11-07)

Question: how can the one-file game reach phones, what does it cost, which store rules bite a web-based game, and which free-to-play model sells nothing that wins fights (P1-03 rejected an in-game economy). Facts below were read on 2026-11-07. "Verified" marks how solid each fact is: yes = read on the official page, partly = official page read through a summary tool or only blogs, no/unknown = not confirmed. Prices are in USD as the stores state them; EUR is shown only where the fact comes from a EUR source (none did). Nothing was installed, no account was created, the game was not touched.

#### A. Ways to put the game on phones
- **A1 Installable web app (PWA / Add to Home Screen), no store.** iPhone: Safari "Add to Home Screen" opens the page as an app when the manifest `display` is `standalone` or `fullscreen`; manifest icons work since iOS 15.4; Web Push since 16.4. Android: Chrome installs a PWA with a manifest and a service worker. Cost: 0, no account, no review, no store cut. Needs the game on an HTTPS address of our own (GitHub Pages is not enabled; making it public needs the owner's OK).
  - Safari deletes script-writable storage (localStorage, IndexedDB, service-worker caches) after 7 days of Safari use without interaction, but Home Screen web apps have their own day counter and are not expected to lose data. Saves in Safari and in the Home Screen app are separate stores (blog source, partly).
  - Sources: https://webkit.org/blog/13878/web-push-for-web-apps-on-ios-and-ipados/ (2023-02-16), https://webkit.org/blog/10218/full-third-party-cookie-blocking-and-more/ (2020-03-24), https://www.magicbell.com/blog/pwa-ios-limitations-safari-support-complete-guide
  - Verified: yes for the WebKit facts; partly for the cross-store save split and the iOS offline-flakiness reports (blogs only).
- **A2 Google Play via Trusted Web Activity (TWA, tool Bubblewrap).** The Android app just opens our hosted PWA fullscreen in Chrome (Chrome 72+); the app and the site must come from the same developer, proved with Digital Asset Links. Needs the PWA hosted on a domain we control, so it depends on A1's hosting. Bubblewrap needs Node 18+. Play reportedly requires an Android App Bundle (.aab) and Play App Signing, and says TWA is not for apps aimed at children under 13 (blog source).
  - Sources: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/android/trusted-web-activity/, https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/bubblewrap/blob/main/README.md, https://vaadin.com/blog/submitting-a-pwa-to-google-play-store-using-bubblewrap
  - Verified: yes for what TWA is and the Chrome/Node versions; partly for .aab, signing and the kids limit (blogs).
- **A3 Capacitor wrapper (Android and iOS).** Packs the page inside a native WebView app: no hosting needed, works offline because the file ships inside the app. Capacitor's current docs: iOS 15+ and Xcode 26+ required; Android API 24+ (Android 7+), WebView 60+, built with Android Studio. The project wants a `package.json` and a web folder with `index.html`, i.e. a small build folder around our one file (the game file itself stays one file; no code change). Buying anything inside needs a native billing plugin (A5).
  - iPhone builds need macOS for Xcode; from Windows the usual route is a cloud Mac build service (Capgo Build, Capawesome Cloud, Codemagic, Bitrise named; vendor marketing, prices not read) and an Apple Developer account.
  - Sources: https://capacitorjs.com/docs/getting-started, https://capacitorjs.com/docs/ios, https://capacitorjs.com/docs/android, https://capawesome.io/blog/how-to-build-and-deploy-ios-apps-without-a-mac/
  - Verified: yes for versions; partly for Windows cloud-build route (vendor pages); unknown: cloud build prices and Capacitor's licence line (not on the pages read; widely known as MIT, not confirmed here).
- **A4 itch.io (browser and itch app).** HTML5 upload is a ZIP with `index.html` at its root, or a single `.html` file that references nothing else (our file qualifies). Limits: 1,000 files, 500 MB total, 200 MB per file, paths relative, outside requests HTTPS. Turn on "Mobile Friendly" so phone visitors get a "Click to launch in fullscreen" button. By default HTML5 games take payments only as donations; to sell, set Kind of Game to "Downloadable" (page sets suggest the paid build would then be a download, not an in-browser play; that part is a guess: verified partly). Pay-what-you-want with a minimum of 0 is allowed.
  - Sources: https://itch.io/docs/creators/html5, https://itch.io/docs/creators/faq
  - Verified: yes.
- **A5 Selling inside a wrapped app.** Apple rule 3.1.1: unlocks of content or features must use Apple In-App Purchase; own license keys, QR codes or crypto are not allowed. Random-item purchases ("loot boxes") must show the odds before purchase. Google has its own billing system (Play Billing). In both a wrapped game needs a native billing plugin and a small bridge call from the page (feature-detect, no effect in a plain browser).
  - Source: https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/ (3.1.1 read through a summary tool, not word for word)
  - Verified: partly.

#### B. Costs
Costs (read 2026-11-07):

| Item | Cost | Source | Verified |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Developer Program | 99 USD per year (Enterprise 299, not relevant) | https://developer.apple.com/programs/ | yes |
| Apple fee waiver | only nonprofits, accredited schools, governments; not individuals | https://developer.apple.com/help/account/membership/fee-waivers | yes |
| Google Play developer account | 25 USD one time | https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6112435 | yes |
| Year one both stores | about 124 USD; later years 99 USD (Apple only) | sum of the two rows | yes |
| Apple commission, Small Business Program | 15% on paid apps and IAP, for developers up to 1 M USD proceeds in the prior year (and new developers) | https://developer.apple.com/app-store/small-business-program/ | yes; standard (non-small-business) rate not shown on the page I read, commonly stated as 30%, unverified |
| Google Play commission | Pages differ by region: older rule 15% on the first 1 M USD per year, 30% above; the page now also lists a newer scheme for first installs on/after 2026-06-30 in the EEA, UK, US (rows like 20% or 25% plus a 5% billing fee; the table came back flattened, so which row applies to a small paid game is not confirmed) | https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/112622 | partly; re-read before pricing |
| itch.io | default 10% revenue share (0 to 100% adjustable) plus PayPal/Stripe fee 2.9% + 0.30 USD per sale; payouts need 5 USD minimum, tax interview (30% withholding without Tax ID) | https://itch.io/docs/creators/payments | yes |
| PWA / own hosting | 0 on GitHub Pages (needs owner OK); own domain not priced here | n/a | unknown |
| Cloud Mac builds for iPhone | not priced (vendors only) | A3 sources | unknown |

Rough take-home for a 4.00 EUR sale (my arithmetic, not a source): store prices include VAT; at about 21% VAT the base is about 3.31; after a 15% store cut about 2.81. itch.io: about 3.18 before VAT handling (10% = 0.40 EUR; processor 2.9% + 0.30 USD, about 0.42 EUR together, converted at about 1 USD = 0.92 EUR); how itch.io handles EU VAT was not checked.

#### C. Store rules that affect a web-based game
- **Apple 4.2 Minimum Functionality.** "If your app is not particularly useful, unique, or 'app-like,' it doesn't belong on the App Store"; 4.2.2 names web clippings and link collections. Developer forums quote Apple rejecting apps "not sufficiently different from a mobile browsing experience" and telling them to ship a web app instead. A fully playable 3D game with touch controls, saves, offline play and sound is a game, not a web clipping, which is the usual way wrapped games pass; still a real review risk for a bare WebView. Reduce it with offline start, no visible browser chrome, no web links out, and (if cheap) a native touch like haptics. Sources: https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/ (summary), https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/95085, https://www.mobiloud.com/blog/app-store-review-guidelines-webview-wrapper. Verified: partly.
- **Apple 4.7 (mini apps / HTML5 mini games)** is written for apps that host other people's mini games; summary shows it asks for privacy rules, content filtering, report/block and age-restriction. Our own game is not a host, so it likely does not apply; confirm on the live guideline text. Verified: partly.
- **Apple 4.2.6 templates:** apps from commercial app-generator services are rejected unless submitted by the content owner; hand-made Capacitor is not a template. Verified: partly.
- **Apple 1.3 Kids:** a Kids-category app may not carry ads, third-party analytics, outside links or purchases without a parental gate. The game is a fighting game, so do not aim at Kids. Verified: yes (verbatim).
- **Apple 2.5.2:** an app may not download code that changes its features. The game is bundled in the app, so fine; loading it from a web address in the app would be the risk. Verified: yes (verbatim).
- **Apple EU:** from 2026-10-01 unified EU terms replace Core Technology Fee with a 5% Core Technology Commission for alternative marketplaces / Web Distribution; App Store commission in the EU is 26% standard, 15% small business (IAP). Web Distribution is an alternative to the App Store worth knowing, not researched further. Source: https://developer.apple.com/support/dma-and-apps-in-the-eu/. Verified: partly; re-read before pricing (these dates and rates differ from Apple's mid-2025 announcement of a 5% fee from 2026-01-01; read 2026-11-07).
- **Google Play, new personal accounts** (created after 2023-11-13): a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before production access; Google's review of the request takes about 7 days. Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465. Verified: yes.
- **Google Play target level:** since 2026-08-31 new apps and updates must target Android 16 (API 36) (extension to 2026-11-01 has passed). Wrapper tools must be current. Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/11926878. Verified: yes.
- **Android developer verification:** from 2026-09-30 apps installed on certified devices (sideloaded ones included) in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand need a verified developer; more regions in 2027+. Hobbyist "limited distribution" accounts reach at most 20 devices, no ID, no fee; power users keep an "advanced flow" to sideload unverified apps. This matters for a direct APK from itch.io, not for Play. Source: https://developer.android.com/developer-verification, https://www.theregister.com/2025/08/26/android_developer_verification_sideloading. Verified: partly (what applies to APK downloads in the EU was not confirmed).
- **Privacy and age rating:** Play needs a Data Safety form and Apple needs an age-rating answer and, as far as I know, a privacy-policy link; fighting violence raises the rating. The game collects no data today (saves stay on the device), so the forms should be short. Not read on official pages: unknown.

#### D. Free-to-play models that fit a fighter without pay-to-win
- **D1 Free game + one-time "Supporter pack" (cosmetics only).** Rushdown Revolt moved to free-to-play and made its pack a fully optional cosmetic supporter pack, with earlier buyers getting a bonus skin; Thrillkings' supporter DLC is cosmetics with no gameplay effect and unlocks at once. In Breakpoint terms: extra outfits/colours for the character creator, a credits line, nothing in the fight. Fits P1-03. Source: https://www.dekudeals.com/items/rushdown-revolt-golden-supporter-pack, https://www.dekudeals.com/items/thrillkings-golden-supporter-pack. Verified: partly (store listings only).
- **D2 Free to start, one-time full unlock.** First part free (for example Arcade early levels, Training, a few fighters), one purchase of about 3 to 5 EUR opens everything. It gates content, not fight power, so it does not break the P1-03 rule; simplest to understand and matches the friend's "pay about 3-5 EUR once if it caught me". Risk: a free build that feels cut down. No source; my judgment.
- **D3 Premium: one price, no free part.** Streets of Rage 4 mobile (Playdigious, 2022-05-24) launched at 7.99 USD with no ads; a DLC chapter is 2.99 USD; deal trackers show it often at 1.99 USD. Premium needs a store page that sells itself and is a hard sell for an unknown title. Sources: https://gematsu.com/2022/03/streets-of-rage-4-coming-to-ios-android-on-may-24, https://www.apppricinglab.com/app/apple/1601446687. Verified: partly.
- **D4 Free with ads.** Not recommended: ad SDKs are outside code (the project allows none), interrupt a 60 Hz fight, and Apple's Kids rule forbids ads in Kids apps. No ad income figure was found, so the money side is unknown.
- **D5 Cosmetic shop with random packs.** Rejected by P1-03 and a rule problem: random purchases need odds shown on Apple.
- **What comparable mobile fighters do:** Skullgirls mobile is free with in-app purchases (10 listed), console/PC is paid; Brawlhalla is free-to-play; Shadow Fight 3/4 and Punch Club pricing was not found (unknown). Sources: https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/id1280762571, https://apppricinglab.com/iap/apple/1280762571, https://www.esports.net/news/fighting-games/is-skullgirls-free/. Verified: partly.
- **Player mood:** the free-to-play fighter 2XKO drew heavy complaints about high skin prices; fans of Rivals of Aether II reportedly praised that every skin can be earned in reasonable time without paying (no source read for this part). Lesson: if cosmetics are sold, keep prices low and keep an earn-by-playing route. Source: https://dashfight.com/news/prices-for-2-xko-microtransactions-are-causing-a-stir-in-the-community-7921. Verified: partly (news and forums, anecdotal).

#### E. itch.io versus stores
- itch.io: no review, no yearly fee, 10% share by default (adjustable), ready for the single file today, PWA/Add to Home Screen possible from a page we host, but the HTML5 build there is donation-only unless sold as a download. Best for early players, feedback and the friend test; weakest at discovery on phones.
- Play Store: 25 USD once, 12 testers for 14 days first, real discovery and billing. Apple App Store: 99 USD per year, needs a Mac build route, review risk 4.2, best discovery among phone buyers. Neither store is free of a cut on in-app sales.
- Consequence for the friend's picture ("a free mobile game, download it"): "download" means a store icon. The Home Screen route gives an icon too but no store listing.

#### F. What the game needs before a store release (checked against the code on 2026-11-07, read-only)
- Present now: `viewport-fit=cover`, safe-area handling, apple web-app meta tags, WebGL context-loss listener (line 2048), `visibilitychange` handler, AudioContext, fullscreen helper, saves in localStorage, 1.18 MB file (1,178,607 LF bytes) (budget 4 MB, LF count).
- Missing for a PWA: no `<link rel="manifest">`, no service worker. A service worker and a manifest need their own URLs, so offline PWA means two tiny extra files beside the HTML (needs a DECIDE against "one file"; a data-URL manifest may not meet install rules, unverified). A wrapper (A3) needs neither.
- Saves: localStorage is wiped if the user clears site data; Safari and Home Screen copies are separate. Add an export/import save code or file before shipping to two places; test a save that survives a wrapper update (P16-02 migration test is already planned).
- Touch-only flows: every menu, tutorial, character creator and online lobby must run with no keyboard or mouse; back-button/swipe-from-bottom gestures on iPhone can close the game mid-fight (blog report), so test pause on `visibilitychange` and an on-screen pause. Phone widths 390x844 and 844x390 already in the checks; add one with notches and the Home Screen mode.
- Audio: iOS/Chrome allow sound only after a first tap; confirm resume of the context after a call or app switch.
- Low-spec performance: use the P0-04 method (640x360, CPU throttle 4, quality low) on a real older Android and an older iPhone; P15-01 profiling already planned. Handle WebGL context loss when switching apps on iPhone (blog report) with a rebuild path, not just a listener.
- Legal/store pages: icon set (192/512, maskable), screenshots, privacy policy page, age-rating answers, credits (P16-04); no analytics or ads keeps forms short.
- Online mode: wrapped apps need network permission handling and a clear offline message.

#### Inputs for P18-15 (Steam price)
- Friend's willingness: free to download, about 3-5 EUR if it caught their interest (2026-11-02). One person; not a market test.
- Mobile anchors: Streets of Rage 4 mobile 7.99 USD at launch, often 1.99 USD; free-to-play with cosmetics is the norm for mobile fighters. A premium mobile price above about 5 EUR looks hard for an unknown title.
- Cut taken: Apple small-business 15% (standard rate unconfirmed), Google 15% on older rule but a newer scheme exists (re-read), itch.io 10% + processor fee. Steam's own fee and listing cost were not part of this task.
- Keep Steam at least as high as the mobile one-time unlock, so a cheap phone version does not undercut it; a free mobile base with a 3-5 EUR unlock suggests a Steam price in the same band or a little above, to be set from comparable Steam fighters in P18-15.
- Decide first whether the paid part is "supporter pack" (D1), "full unlock" (D2) or "premium" (D3); the Steam price follows from that choice.

Recommendation and open questions: Appendix C, P18-26 mobile release recommendation (2026-11-07).

## P18-27 - How fighters ease new players in (researched 2026-11-07)

One entry per game: how it lowers the entry barrier, in our own words, only what a source confirmed. All pages were read on 2026-11-07 (WebSearch standard mode, then WebFetch). "Seen in search only" means the page was in a search result but could not be fetched (blocked or cut off), so it counts as unverified. The decision that uses this entry is P18-27 (Appendix C).

#### Street Fighter 6 (Modern controls)
- Two schemes: Classic keeps the six-button layout of earlier games; Modern is a simplified four-button layout where a special move is one button plus a direction. Verified: yes.
- Modern is the default control type on first launch (World Tour and the Battle Hub start on it), and the player can switch to Classic in the game's settings. Verified: partly (one third-party guide read in full; no Capcom page); partly for the other guides (search snippets only; two more pages were cut off).
- Cost of Modern: press and community posts report that specials done with Modern's one-button shortcut do about 20 percent less damage (typed-in specials reportedly keep full damage; not confirmed on a page read) (the article read calls it 80 percent damage scaling). The developers, in the page read, call Modern an alternative way to play, not an easier or stronger one, and say it suits some characters well and others badly. Capcom's own wording for the damage figure was not found. Verified: partly.
- Lesson used: the easy scheme is a choice the player can leave, with the same fight rules underneath, and it carries a price so that skill still pays.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_6 (read 2026-11-07); https://gameranx.com/features/id/467807/article/street-fighter-6-how-to-switch-to-classic-controls/ (read 2026-11-07); https://dashfight.com/news/street-fighter-6-developers-reveal-controversy-over-modern-controls-4366 (read 2026-11-07); damage figure seen in search only: https://esports.gg/guides/street-fighter-6/do-modern-controls-do-less-damage-in-sf6
- Verified: partly (default and layout yes; damage figure is secondary press, not Capcom)

#### Tekken 8 (Special Style)
- Special Style maps each button to a recommended move or combo for the character, so a newcomer can use combos without exact inputs. The director said it is meant to make the game feel more like an action game for newcomers. Verified: yes.
- It can be switched on or off at any point of a match with one button (default: the top-left shoulder button; keyboard O). Verified: yes (two pages). "Even mid-combo or while being hit" appeared only in a low-quality search result and the two pages that were read say they do not state it, so it is not used. Verified: no.
- The director gave no view on a damage penalty or on tournament use. Verified: yes (what he did not say).
- Auto-combos are described as far from optimal, so strong players still do it by hand; Harada is reported to say even experienced players use the single button for a hard input under pressure (for example a Rage Art) and as a way to learn a new character's plan. Other reviews (seen in search only) say the style hits a skill ceiling quickly. Verified: partly.
- Not found and dropped: that it descends from an easy-combo assist of Tekken 7; that it is easy to punish for a player who knows the game.
- Lesson used: the assist is a switch the player can flip at any moment, and its ceiling is low by design.
- Sources: https://eventhubs.com/news/2023/aug/31/special-style-tekken-8-director (read 2026-11-07); https://www.shacknews.com/article/138480/tekken-8-turn-off-special-style (read 2026-11-07); https://destructoid.com/how-to-turn-off-special-style-in-tekken-8 (read 2026-11-07); https://press-start.com.au/?p=143834 (read 2026-11-07)
- Verified: partly

#### Tekken 8 (Arcade Quest)
- A mode with a created avatar and a mentor (Max) who explains the basics: demonstrations first, then practice at your own pace, then fights against computer opponents through arcades toward a championship. Harada said it differs from earlier arcade modes because it welcomes unskilled players. Verified: yes.
- One page calls it a single-player mode; another describes it as the online mode's lobby with arcades, avatars, online battles and tournaments, so the exact shape (offline, online or both) is unknown and not used. Verified: no.
- Reviews are split: some praise the tutorial, others (seen in search only) call it a slog or too heavy on tutorial. The decision therefore says "reviews are mixed", not "reviews praise". Verified: partly (search snippets only).
- Lesson used: teaching inside play works, but a long lesson is a risk; keep the lines short and shown once.
- Sources: https://realsport101.com/tekken/tekken-8-arcade-quest-game-mode (read 2026-11-07); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekken_8 (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 characters); reviews seen in search only: https://www.techradar.com/gaming/tekken-8-review, https://stevivor.com/reviews/tekken-8-review-strike-a-pose/
- Verified: partly

#### Tekken 8 (Heat)
- Heat is a timed state that gives a character extra moves and chip damage and some changed move properties (for example a guard break); it is a comeback and aggression system. Used only in "Inputs for P18-14". Verified: yes.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekken_8 (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 characters)
- Verified: yes

#### Super Smash Bros. series
- Two attack buttons: one for normal attacks and one for special attacks; a held direction picks which move comes out; no quarter-circle style motions. The article says the controls are simpler than other fighting games and that the series was meant as an alternative to combo-heavy fighters. Verified: yes.
- Lesson used: a small button set with direction as the modifier is enough for a big move list; the learning cost lies in the layers, not the inputs.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Smash_Bros. (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 characters)
- Verified: yes

#### Fantasy Strike
- Designed by Sirlin Games to be easier to learn: it removes motion inputs and redundant moves and can be played with a stick and three buttons, while the makers aim to keep the strategy of a traditional fighter. Reviews mostly praise the balance of access and depth; some say the simple design and small move sets cost depth, and the roster is small. Verified: yes.
- Lesson used: the simplicity is built into the game for everyone (no separate mode), which is the same bet as our Easy-to-enter, deep-to-master rule. Reviews also show the risk: too little to learn reads as shallow, so our depth layers stay.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Strike (read 2026-11-07)
- Verified: yes

#### Claims checked and dropped from P18-27
- SF6: "some options are not available on Modern" (replaced by the sourced damage cost, partly); the old text is gone.
- Tekken 8: "even mid-hit"; "descended from Tekken 7's easy-combo assist"; "easy to punish for a player who knows the game"; "a few people say the best on-ramp is a short hand-held tutorial never called a tutorial". Not sourced.
- "Brawlers with a few buttons (Fighting Force, Dynamite Cop, Def Jam) teach with the first stage itself": Appendix B (P1-01) holds their mechanics but nothing about teaching, so the claim is dropped; the point that Arcade on Easy is the first fight stays as our own reading of the game.
- Tekken neutral guard (Tekken 2 onward): already in Appendix B, P1-01, Tekken (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekken), verified partly there.

## P18-14 - What the closest games do for identity (researched 2026-11-07)

One entry per game: the feature that gives it identity, or the mechanic an X-factor option would compete with, in our own words, only what a source confirmed. All pages were read on 2026-11-07 (WebSearch standard mode, then WebFetch; WebFetch returns a short answer made from the page text, and for long Wikipedia pages it read only the first 100,000 characters, so "not stated" means "not in the part read"). "Seen in search only" means the page was in a search result but was not fetched, so it counts as unverified. The decision that uses this entry is P18-14 (Appendix C). Games already written up in P1-01 (Tekken, Dead or Alive, Virtua Fighter, Mortal Kombat, Urban Reign) and in P18-27 (SF6 Modern, Tekken 8 Special Style and Arcade Quest, Smash, Fantasy Strike) are not repeated; only what P18-14 needs beyond them is added.

The question asked of every source: does this game have (a) a feature a newcomer meets in the first minute and an expert still plays with, (b) a named mechanic that makes the game recognisable, (c) anything that works like a chain reaction in the scenery, a police or heat clock, a copy of the player's habits, or a timing-defence signature.

#### Dead or Alive (environment: Danger Zones)
- The series has interactive stage parts called Danger Zones; a fighter caught in one takes extra damage, and at low health a Danger Zone is more likely to knock a fighter out than a normal attack. Hazards range from falls to explosives to breakable structures. Verified: yes.
- Dead or Alive 2 made stages larger and multi-tiered and replaced the explosive ring edges with fully interactive zones (falls, electrified and explosive walls, breakable walls, windows); Dead or Alive 3 expanded the multi-tier idea; Dead or Alive 4 added moving obstacles, which a well-timed counter hold can avoid. Verified: yes.
- The article does not describe one environment effect setting off another (chain reaction): not stated in the first 100,000 of 178,659 characters. Verified: partly (absence in the part read).
- Lesson used: single-trigger hazards with extra damage are the genre's standard form of environment play; the game's identity claim for scenery has to be something more than "the stage hurts".
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_or_Alive_(franchise) (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 characters)
- Verified: yes (danger zones); partly (no chain reaction)

#### Def Jam: Fight for NY (environment and crowd)
- The game stresses using the environment and the surrounding crowd to hurt: throw an opponent against barriers, slam a head, ram a door or gate; wall slams can finish an opponent whose consciousness is very low. Verified: yes.
- The crowd shoves a thrown or close fighter back into the fight, sometimes holds a fighter open to attack, and some spectators carry weapons and hand them over. Verified: yes.
- Momentum builds from successful moves, counters and taunting at a rate tied to Charisma (a created fighter's clothing, tattoos and jewellery set it); a full meter allows a Blazin' Taunt and then a Blazin' Move. The article does not say Blazin' Moves use the environment. Verified: yes.
- Fighters pick one, two or three of five styles (Streetfighting, Kickboxing, Martial Arts, Wrestling, Submissions); each style has its own finisher for a fighter in danger. Verified: yes.
- One hazard setting off another is not stated. Verified: yes (what it does not say).
- Lesson used: the closest "urban" fighter makes identity from the crowd and the setting as a whole, not from one mechanic, and the momentum meter is its comeback and spectacle system (ours is the Momentum gauge, P18-08).
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Jam:_Fight_for_NY (read 2026-11-07)
- Verified: yes

#### Injustice: Gods Among Us and Mortal Kombat X (interactive objects)
- Injustice stages have several areas with interactive objects; what an object does depends on whether the fighter is a power or a gadget character (Batman puts a bomb on a car; Superman lifts it as a weapon); a heavy hit near a corner launches the foe into a new section of the stage (a transition); players can turn interactive elements and transitions off. Verified: yes.
- Injustice's Clash is a wager: after the first life bar is lost, both players secretly commit part of their super meter and the higher bid wins, with a cutscene. Verified: yes.
- Mortal Kombat X lets fighters use scenery to reposition and pick up objects as weapons (compared in the article with Injustice); X-Ray moves cost the whole three-part meter, the same meter pays enhanced specials and combo breakers; each fighter has three variations with different move sets. Verified: yes.
- Neither article describes a chain reaction between objects (single car explosion, single weapon use only): not stated in the first 100,000 characters of each. Verified: partly.
- Lesson used: interactive objects are common in big-budget fighters and are single-step, per-character and switchable off; "the scenery" alone is not a new idea.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injustice:_Gods_Among_Us (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 of 222,526 characters); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortal_Kombat_X (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 of 151,357 characters)
- Verified: yes (objects, clash, meter); partly (no chain reaction)

#### Super Smash Bros. (stage hazards)
- A stage hazard is any stage part that can threaten players; most deal damage and knockback, others move the stage or the camera. The page lists 18 kinds (static, blast, launchers, trapdoors, transformations, weather, vehicles, switches, enemies, stage bosses and others). In Ultimate hazards can be turned off. Verified: yes.
- The page names a few one-step triggers: a switch (the POW Block) must be hit before its changes happen; weather follows a stage transformation; some trapdoors open when a player takes damage; a vehicle collision may set off an explosion on certain items. It describes no general chain system. Verified: yes.
- Lesson used: Smash is the nearest genre example of a hazard that starts another event, and it is a handful of hand-made cases; a rule that chains by material (arc, paper, fire, deck, crush) is a different thing, which is our Appendix C rules matrix R1 to R9.
- Sources: https://www.ssbwiki.com/Stage_hazard (read 2026-11-07)
- Verified: yes

#### Tekken 8 (Heat, stage destruction, Super Ghost Battle)
- Heat is a timed state with chip damage, extra move sets and some changed move properties (a guard break among them); how it is entered is not stated on the page, and the duration is not given. Rage returns with changes; Rage Drive became the Heat Smash. Verified: yes.
- Harada said the game would be more aggressive than Tekken 7 and reward the attacker; a later patch pushing offence drew community criticism and an emergency patch added defensive options. Verified: yes.
- Stage destruction: some stages have harder walls and floors that need several heavy hits to break; on others explosives on the walls and floors send damaged opponents upward; Harada said the game focuses on stage destruction and the characters' reactions to it. Verified: yes.
- Arcade Quest is described here as the online mode's lobby with arcades and avatars, and Harada said it was designed to welcome unskilled players (P18-27 holds the other reading of the mode). Verified: yes.
- Super Ghost Battle is only listed on this page as a mode of the December 2023 demo; the detail is in the next entry. Verified: yes.
- Lesson used: the biggest 3D fighter's identity moves are a comeback state (Heat/Rage) and stage destruction; a comeback state is the P18-08 ultimate in our plan, and destruction is the P18-12 environment work.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekken_8 (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 of 138,567 characters)
- Verified: yes

#### Tekken 8 Super Ghost Battle, Smash Figure Players, Virtua Fighter 4 Evolution (an AI that fights like a player)
- Super Ghost Battle (Tekken 8): an AI opponent the guide says learns how you fight and replicates your style; it tracks how you move, which attacks you use and how you use them, and builds a ghost that fights like you; you can also download other players' ghosts online (in a Fight Lounge) and fight CPU ghosts of several ranks; playing against your own ghost shows you the gaps in your game; if you fight with a different character than your ghost's, it does not learn from those matches. The guide says it unlocks after some Arcade Quest progress (other sources disagree; not used). Verified: yes (one guide; the AI method is not described, and sources disagree on the unlock step).
- Smash Bros. Figure Players (amiibo): in Smash 4 a Figure Player picks up techniques as it levels and copies habits it sees (the page's example: a player who often camps with long-range attacks gets an amiibo that begins to do the same); in Ultimate it learns from its own battles and adapts within a match; level cap 50; learning can be turned off; the page also says Figure Players follow an if-then script and behave very differently from human players. Verified: yes.
- Virtua Fighter 4 Evolution: the article says Sega took the top tournament players from the arcade version and captured their style of play for the AI of a player's opponents in Quest Mode; it does not describe training your own fighter and does not say the AI adapts to the player. A search snippet from fan forums says the game lets you train your own AI fighter through sparring and send it into Arcade and Kumite; that was not read on a page and is not used. Verified: yes (Wikipedia statement); no (the fan claim).
- Lesson used: "an AI that fights like a real person" has precedent in three games, so it cannot be the claim of uniqueness; what none of the pages describes is carrying such a fighter as a short text code that needs no server, which is the only new part of an Echo option.
- Sources: https://www.ggrecon.com/guides/tekken-8-super-ghost-battle (read 2026-11-07); https://www.ssbwiki.com/Figure_Player (read 2026-11-07); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtua_Fighter_4 (read 2026-11-07); fan claim seen in search only: https://host.virtuafighter.com/threads/vf4-evo-ai-training.14691
- Verified: partly

#### Timing-defence signatures: Street Fighter III parry, Garou Just Defend, Sifu structure and parry, Street Fighter 6
- Street Fighter III: a parry deflects an incoming attack without damage if input at the exact moment the attack is about to hit (toward or down); it also works against specials and Super Arts, which would otherwise still cause chip damage; it leaves the attacker open to a counter; the article says it needs precise timing and does not give the frame window or the cost. Verified: yes.
- Garou: Mark of the Wolves: Just Defend rewards a block at the last possible moment with a small health recovery and the ability to counterattack at once, even during block stun; it was designed to go with the Guard Crush system. Verified: yes.
- Sifu: both the player and enemies have a structure gauge; when it fills the guard breaks and the target can be finished; blocking fills your own gauge; evading or parrying is possible and a parry stuns the enemy or throws it in a chosen direction. The article also describes objects as improvised weapons and kicking enemies off ledges. Verified: yes.
- Street Fighter 6: the article says the Drive Gauge builds on earlier mechanics such as parries; it does not describe the Drive Parry's timing, effect or cost, so none of that is used; Burnout (an emptied Drive Gauge: no gauge use, chip damage on block) is described. Verified: yes (Burnout); no (Drive Parry detail, dropped).
- Tekken: some characters can catch and reverse attacks (P1-01, read 2026-10-28; not re-read today). Verified: partly.
- Lesson used: a shared timing window for defence is established in 2D fighters (SF III, Garou) and in a 3D brawler (Sifu), so "perfect timing" is a strength to keep and teach but not an unclaimed identity. Breakpoint's own detail, one window and one button for both Block and Sway fighters (P18-02, P18-27), is not described by any source read; whether any 3D fighter does the same is unknown.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_III (read 2026-11-07); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garou:_Mark_of_the_Wolves (read 2026-11-07); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifu_(video_game) (read 2026-11-07); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_6 (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 of 128,840 characters)
- Verified: yes (SF III, Garou, Sifu); partly (Tekken)

#### Sifu (a single systemic hook as identity)
- Death ages the protagonist several years: older versions hit harder and have less health, some abilities are lost on death, and once the pendant that resurrects you breaks, the next death ends the run. GameSpot singled the aging mechanic out as inventive and IGN called the game uncompromising in design; reception also names the learning curve and replayability, and criticises the camera, a grindy structure and short length. Single-player only. Verified: yes.
- Lesson used: one systemic hook that touches every fight (here, death has a price that changes your stats) is what reviewers remember a small brawler by; the hook is part of how the whole game is played, not a mode. P1-03 (Appendix B) already rejected "aging on death" because it duplicates the Age slider (P6-04), and copying another game's hook is against the rule of our own design, which is why it is not one of the options.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifu_(video_game) (read 2026-11-07)
- Verified: yes

#### Grand Theft Auto (a police clock: the wanted level)
- Crimes raise a wanted level shown in stars (hitting a pedestrian can give one star; harming police gives more); higher levels bring stronger responses, from a few police cars up to tanks and attack helicopters at five or six stars; evading detection or paying at certain places clears it; dying removes it. Verified: yes.
- No search result or page read names a fighting game in which police, sirens or heat from destruction end or limit a fight. Two searches (2026-11-07) found none; absence in two searches is not proof. Verified: partly.
- Lesson used: a heat clock is established in open-world games; as a fighting-game rule it is new in the sources read, but it is a rule that limits the thing the owner praised (scenery), which is a design cost, not a bonus.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_(video_game_series) (read 2026-11-07, first 100,000 of 248,234 characters)
- Verified: yes (wanted system); partly (no fighting game found)

#### Shadow Fight 2 (the nearest mobile fighter)
- A 2D game with fully silhouetted, physics-animated fighters; best-of-three matches against computer opponents with RPG upgrades; seven provinces each ending in a boss; the setting draws on Imperial China, Feudal Japan and Rajput states with demons, gates of shadows and magical abilities; energy limits play to five fights before a refill by waiting, paying or watching ads; on iOS, Android, Windows 8, Switch. Verified: yes.
- Lesson used: the best-known mobile fighter's identity is its art (silhouettes) and its fantasy setting; Breakpoint is 3D and Modern Urban only (owner rule), so the two do not compete on identity. It also means an option named "Shadow ..." would collide with that franchise's name; the Appendix C option is called Echo.
- Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Fight_2 (read 2026-11-07)
- Verified: yes

#### What the owner and the friend wrote (our own records, not web sources)
- Owner, 2026-11-01 (Appendix A, REFERENCE line 180 to 186): likes the new levels and "the interaction with objects in the environment", wants "this aspect developed further, as it adds another layer to the gameplay"; the main thing missing is "an X-factor: one genuinely unique feature that gives the game its own identity". Friend, 2026-11-02 (passed on by the owner, line 241): if it "can establish its own identity within the 2D fighting genre, perhaps with a more accessible approach compared to games like Tekken, I think there could be potential" (the game stays 3D, Appendix A line 86). Verified: yes (read from the file).

#### Inputs for P18-14 (the options weighed in Appendix C)
- A Easy to enter (P18-27; SF6 Modern, Tekken 8 Special Style, Fantasy Strike). B The Beat (SF III parry, Garou Just Defend, Sifu). C Street Chain (DOA, Def Jam, Injustice, MKX, Smash hazards, Tekken 8: single-step scenery only). D Echo (Super Ghost Battle, Figure Players, VF4 Evo). E Sirens (GTA wanted level; no fighting game found).

#### Claims checked and dropped from P18-14
- "No fighting game has chain reactions in the scenery": cannot be shown by absence. Six articles (Dead or Alive, Def Jam FFNY, Injustice, Mortal Kombat X, Smash hazards, Sifu) do not describe it in the part read; the decision therefore says "not found in six sources read", never "no game has it".
- "Wanted-level mechanics have appeared in a fighting game": not found; no claim made.
- SF6 Drive Parry timing and cost: the Wikipedia article read does not give them; not used. (P18-27's SF6 Modern entry is unchanged.)
- VF4 Evolution "train your own AI that learns your style": fan-forum snippets in search only; the Wikipedia article says only that Quest Mode AI copies top players' styles; the fan claim is dropped.
- Smash amiibo "copy the human player's style": the Smash 4 page supports habit copying; Ultimate learns from its own battles; a forum post in search said they do not imitate you. Only the page statements are used.
- Tekken 8 Heat trigger and duration: not on the page read; not used.
- Searches for "chain reaction" in fighting games returned platformer and brawler pages (a bomb-block page, an itch.io devlog); the devlog was seen in search only and is not used.

## P18-54 - Story tropes of the reference games (researched 2026-11-09)

Read: public wiki pages, review sites and recap articles found by web search (sources below). Summaries are paraphrased; no names, places, plots or lines are taken into Breakpoint. Supernatural material is listed only to mark it as left out.

| Game | Setup in one line (paraphrased) | Tropes it uses |
|---|---|---|
| Tekken | A rich family's company runs a world tournament; the prize is often the company itself; father and son try to kill each other over it | tournament with an owner who has his own reasons; family feud over a company; the prize is power, not a trophy; the old man who keeps coming back; every fighter enters for a private reason (supernatural left out: inherited demon power, creatures) |
| Urban Reign | A fighter for hire comes to a city to sort out a gang mess for one boss, and the turf war climbs from street crews to corrupt officials | crew war over districts; hired outsider; each district has its own crew and boss; corruption that goes up a level each act; a partner who fights beside you |
| Def Jam: Fight for NY | The player saves a crew boss from crooked cops and climbs his underground fight clubs against a rival boss's clubs across the city | underground fight clubs owned by bosses; taking clubs one by one; crew members who defect; trash talk before fights; the final fight in the rival boss's own home |
| Sleeping Dogs | An undercover cop joins a triad through a childhood friend and is trusted by neither side | undercover cop; loyalty tested both ways; the old friend who brings you in; small jobs that grow into a war |
| Like a Dragon / Yakuza (0) | A debt collection goes wrong, a man dies on a disputed plot of land, and the hero is framed and hunted by his own family | debt and the collector; a piece of the city everyone wants; framed hero; sworn brother; fight clubs and side bouts; the hero's boss is in danger because of him |
| Streets of Rage | Ex-officers take on a syndicate that runs the city; in the sequel the boss kidnaps their friend | syndicate owns the city; cops who quit to do it themselves; kidnapped friend; boss's bodyguard as the last gate; one stage per district |
| Final Fight | A new mayor, once a wrestler, sees his daughter kidnapped by the gang that runs the city and goes after them with two friends | kidnapped family member; the gang that runs the city; a crooked businessman at the top of the tower; the final fight at the top floor and a fall from the window; a corrupt cop among the gang |
| Virtua Fighter | A shadowy company holds a world tournament as a cover for its own project; each fighter enters for private reasons (a brother looking for his kidnapped sister) | tournament as a front; sponsor that uses the fighters; searching for a missing sibling; the drunk old master; family style passed down (supernatural left out: a metal fighter) |
| King of Fighters | A bored arms dealer sends invitations to teams of three for his tournament and is the last fight himself | invitation from someone rich and bored; the organiser is the final boss; teams by country; the boss comes back for revenge on the one who beat him (supernatural left out: ancient bloodlines, fire powers) |
| Street Fighter | A crime syndicate's leader holds tournaments to find strong fighters; heroes come from separate paths: a wanderer, a police officer avenging her father, a champion who lost his title | syndicate behind the tournament; revenge for a parent; the champion who lost and wants it back; rivals who respect each other; the boxer who fights for money (supernatural left out: psycho power, fireballs) |
| Sifu | A student hunts the five killers of their master, one boss per location, each with their own crew, ending at the leader | revenge list of names; one boss per place with a crew in front; the boss who was a student of the same school; the choice to spare or finish; the hero ages with every loss (supernatural left out: the talisman that brings you back) |

Shared tropes (games that use them; none supernatural):

| Trope | Games |
|---|---|
| A belt, title or tournament whose owner has his own reasons | Tekken, Virtua Fighter, King of Fighters, Street Fighter |
| Underground fight clubs owned by bosses; climbing them place by place | Def Jam, Like a Dragon, Urban Reign |
| One crew and one boss per district or stage; the crew goes first | Urban Reign, Streets of Rage, Final Fight, Sifu, Def Jam |
| The rival who becomes an ally (or turns on you) | Street Fighter, Def Jam, Tekken, Sleeping Dogs |
| The final fight at the top of the boss's building | Final Fight, Def Jam, Streets of Rage, Sifu |
| The boss who was once the hero's teacher, or taught the champion | Sifu, Tekken, Virtua Fighter |
| The fighter who owes money; the debt collector | Like a Dragon, Street Fighter (the boxer), Def Jam |
| The kidnapped or missing family member | Final Fight, Streets of Rage, Virtua Fighter |
| Revenge for family, with a list of names | Sifu, Street Fighter, Tekken |
| Police family, undercover or ex-cops | Sleeping Dogs, Streets of Rage, Street Fighter, Final Fight (the crooked cop) |
| The old champion's last run | Street Fighter, Tekken, Virtua Fighter |
| Family money behind the fights | Tekken, King of Fighters |
| Fighters from many countries, each with a private reason | Tekken, Virtua Fighter, King of Fighters, Street Fighter |

Left out (supernatural or sci-fi): inherited demon genes and creatures (Tekken), the metal fighter (Virtua Fighter), ancient bloodlines and fire (King of Fighters), psycho power and energy blasts (Street Fighter), the reviving talisman (Sifu).

What makes these stories read as written by people (notes for the voice, no lines copied): the best-loved scenes are short and specific (a single prop, a place, an injury), characters want plain things (money, a family member back, a title), villains are bored, tired or doing a job rather than evil in speeches, rivals talk about themselves rather than about the hero, jokes come from character (a streamer, a baker, a cousin), and the endings are small (one image, often comic) rather than a summary of what was learned.

Sources (read 2026-11-09): Wikipedia / Wikiwand pages for Urban Reign, Def Jam: Fight for NY, Sifu, Sleeping Dogs, Yakuza 0, Final Fight, Streets of Rage 2, Virtua Fighter 4, The King of Fighters '94, Rugal Bernstein; Den of Geek and Red Bull Tekken story recaps (denofgeek.com/games/tekken-the-strange-history-of-the-mishima-family, redbull.com/int-en/tekken-8-story-recap-mishima-family-saga); TV Tropes pages for Virtua Fighter, Def Jam and Final Fight (seen in search results); GameRevolution's Def Jam: Fight for NY feature; Looper's Sifu ending article; Streets of Rage fandom wiki (Mr. X); Street Fighter recaps on svg.com and gamerbraves. TV Tropes' Tournament Arc page refused the fetch (HTTP 403) and is not used.

## P18-15 Steam price research (2026-11-09)

Question: what would people pay on Steam for Breakpoint as it stands today, judged on its content and quality and not marked down for being unfinished. Is EUR 2.99 right, is EUR 5 right if the game is polished, and what about the informal EUR 5-10 opinion. This is a market estimate, not a plan to sell it now; the price stays the owner's choice (the price is also tied to the mobile choice, see P18-26 "Inputs for P18-15").

How it was done: every number below was read on 2026-11-09 from the public Steam store page of each game (German store, so prices are in EUR) and from Steam's public store data (the price lookup and the tag search listings). "List price" is the price without a running sale; a sale price is named only where one was running. The review figure is the score and count Steam shows on the page, which is calculated from reviews in English (the page says "in your language"), so the real all-language count can be higher. Sales numbers of these games are not public; where a sales figure appears it is an estimate and is marked. Nothing was bought, installed or downloaded, no account was used, the game was not touched. Visual quality was judged from store tags and descriptions only, not from screenshots (images were not opened), so the "Look" column is weak evidence. The reviews' text was not read.

### What Breakpoint is today (from SPEC.md and Appendix C, P18-26)
- One HTML file, about 1.2 MB, WebGL, procedural low-poly fighters, no licensed assets. 32 preset fighters, 16 martial-arts styles with their own animations, character creator, 8 levels.
- Modes: Arcade story, Survival, Training, Free Fight, Versus, Tournament (bracket of 8 or 16), up to 4 local players; touch, gamepad and keyboard.
- Not built yet: online play (planned, WebRTC), the open P18 polish tasks, the owner device checks, any outside player feedback.
- Steam needs the game packaged as an app (the file would sit in a wrapper); that is not researched here and would be a DECIDE against the "one file, no dependency" rule.

### A. Comparison: 15 small paid fighters and brawlers on Steam
Chosen as the nearest in size: solo or tiny-team fighters and beat-em-ups, 2D and 3D, low-poly or retro looks, price under about EUR 20. Sorted from cheapest to dearest list price.

Also read, left out of the table: Mayhem Brawler (2D beat-em-up, 19.50, 89% of 844, https://store.steampowered.com/app/1306720), The TakeOver (2D beat-em-up, 13.99, 83% of 1,129, https://store.steampowered.com/app/418620), Fighters Forge (3D arena brawler, Early Access, 9.75, 4 reviews, https://store.steampowered.com/app/2853810) and Fighting Heart (3D 1v1, Early Access, 3.39, 2 reviews, https://store.steampowered.com/app/1868600). The last two have too few reviews to say anything about demand. Wrestling Empire's 94% of 2,644 comes from the Steam tag search listing (the page showed a different 30-day tooltip). Verified: yes (prices, scores and counts as shown on the pages on 2026-11-09); partly (content column: store description and categories only; Look column: tags only).

### B. What the table shows
- **Polished hand-made 2D beat-em-ups sit at EUR 13.99-19.50** with 800-1,200 reviews (Fight'N Rage, Mayhem Brawler, The TakeOver). That is the top of this class and it comes from hand-drawn art and finished design, not from content volume alone.
- **Small one-person 3D fighters and brawlers list at EUR 0.99-6** (Street Fighting Simulator, Drunken Fist, Beatdown Brawler, Revenge of the Boxer, Weekend Warriors MMA). Their review counts are 21-167, mostly under 70. Of these five, the one with the most reviews and best score (Revenge of the Boxer, 90% of 167) is at EUR 4.99. The two at EUR 2.99 (Drunken Fist, Beatdown Brawler) have 56 and 21 reviews, and one of them is Mixed.
- **EUR 8-13 is where online play or a big hand-made roster shows up**: Fight of Animals (online, 8.19), Taekwondo Grand Prix (online, 11.79), Mad Streets (online, 12.49), Fight of Gods (online, 12.99). 4 of the 15 have online, and all 4 list at EUR 8.19 or more. The offline ones at that height (Streets of Fury EX 9.75, Shaolin vs Wutang 11.59, Wrestling Revolution 3D 9.99) are older (2015-2018) and have about 400-960 reviews.
- **Low-poly or retro 3D can sell dear when the content is deep**: Wrestling Empire lists at 19.50 and has 2,644 reviews; Wrestling Revolution 3D at 9.99. This is the closest example that a plain 3D look is not a price ceiling by itself. It is a wrestling simulator with career and booking content that Breakpoint does not match in kind, so it is a ceiling example, not a price Breakpoint should copy.
- Score does not follow price: Beatdown Brawler (2.99) is Mixed, Streets of Fury EX (9.75) is Overwhelmingly Positive. A review score here tells how well the game meets what its page promised.
- No game in this set listed under EUR 8 has more than 170 reviews (the highest is Revenge of the Boxer, 167 at 4.99). Small sample, no statistics; it only suggests that low-priced small fighters on Steam stay small in audience. Estimate.

### C. Sales and money, as estimates
- Sales per review: Simon Carless's "New Boxleiter number" from 237 games with shared figures is about 41 sales per review for games launched in 2020, and it falls each year (people review sooner now); the article warns that the range is wide (some games were reviewed once per 200 sales) and that free games do not fit. Source: https://www.pcgamesn.com/steam/number-of-copies-sold. Estimate: a game like the cheap 3D ones above (20-170 reviews) has sold roughly 800 to 7,000 copies in its lifetime; the real figure can be well off. Unknown for any single game.
- What a copy brings: Steam keeps a share (the commonly stated 30%; the official fee page read does not state it, third-party pages do: https://www.steampageanalyzer.com/blog/steam-pricing-strategy) and the shelf price includes VAT (assumed 20%, my assumption). My arithmetic for a full-price copy: EUR 2.99 gives about 1.75; EUR 4.99 about 2.90; EUR 7.99 about 4.65; EUR 9.99 about 5.85. Sales, regional prices and refunds lower the real average; that article puts the real average near 48% of list before VAT at 9.99 USD.
- Cost to list: Steam charges 100 USD per new game, not refundable, paid back out of the first payment after the game earns 1,000 USD. Source (official): https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/appfee. At EUR 2.99 that is about 50 copies to cover the fee; at EUR 4.99 about 30 (assuming 1 USD is about 0.86 EUR, and counting full-price copies only). The fee is not the hard part; being found is.
- Pricing advice from the same third-party article (a blog, not research): very low prices read as low quality and get scrolled past; the launch price caps later sale prices, so a game is better launched at the price it will be sold at with a 10-15% launch discount than at a "cheap" one that cannot go lower. It describes USD 4.99 as the tier for 1-3 hour experiences and USD 9.99 as the most common indie price. Same URL as above. Verified: partly (one blog; it fits the table but is not proof).

### D. Likely price range for Breakpoint as it stands today (estimate)
For: more content than every 3D game in the table under EUR 8 (32 fighters, 16 styles, creator, 8 levels, 7 modes, up to 4 local players, touch, pad and keyboard); a deep style system; no licensed assets; no ads, no extras to buy.
Against: no online play (4 of 15 comparables have it and all of those list at 8.19 or more); procedural low-poly fighters with no hand-made art, which the table prices at the low and middle band; no outside reviews, no store history, a one-person project; open polish tasks, owner device checks still to do; a touch-first game arriving on a keyboard-and-pad store; the packaging question.
Estimate: **EUR 3.99 to 6.99 as a launch list price, most likely EUR 4.99.** Reasoning: the size of the content puts it at or above the best small 3D games at EUR 4.99-5.99 and clearly above the EUR 2.99 ones, but nothing in the table sells without online and hand-made art above EUR 8 apart from the proven 2D classics and the wrestling giant. A price of EUR 7.99-9.99 is not supported yet. It becomes reasonable only with online play working, a polish pass done and a first set of outside reviews; Streets of Fury EX (offline, 4 local players, 9.75, 96% of 713) shows that the top of the range exists for the content class, but it has hand-drawn art and has been on sale since 2015.

### E. Answers
- **EUR 2.99:** too low for what the game holds today. The content is clearly larger than the two EUR 2.99 games in the table, and the net is about 1.75 a copy. A low price is allowed (the owner said a low figure is fine) and it is the safe "cannot disappoint" choice, but it signals a small game, and as the launch price it leaves no room for a sale. Better use for 2.99: the price in a sale (about 40% off a 4.99 list), or the floor for a mobile unlock.
- **EUR 5 if polished enough:** yes, this is the best-supported answer. 4.99 is the price of the best-reviewed small 3D fighter in the table (Revenge of the Boxer, 90% of 167), it sits just under the EUR 5.99 MMA game, and the one blog read calls it the tier for short experiences; Breakpoint is larger than that tier. "Polished enough" here means: the critical sweep and bug tasks done, no broken menu or fight in a first hour, sound checked, keyboard and gamepad play checked, and the device checks passed.
- **The informal EUR 5-10 opinion:** right as a span, wrong as one price. The lower half (5-6.99) fits today's game once polished; the upper half (7.99-9.99) needs online play and outside reviews first. The friend's EUR 3-5 for a mobile-feeling game is the low end of the same span (one person; not a market test).
- **Mobile (P18-26):** the P18-26 notes say a premium phone price above about EUR 5 looks hard for an unknown title and suggest a free phone base with a one-time unlock of about EUR 3-5, and they set the rule to keep Steam at least as high as the phone unlock. A phone unlock of EUR 3-5 with Steam at EUR 4.99 fits that rule; Steam at EUR 2.99 would force the phone unlock down to about the same.
- **Not decided here:** whether to sell on Steam at all, the wrapper, and any price. The owner picks.
